tagline: Mule-wagon roads cross high passes between abandoned mining towns
intro: The Alpine Loop leaves pavement for rocky roads in the San Juan Mountains, crossing Cinnamon and Engineer passes. Colorado’s transportation department lists 63 miles and four to six hours of driving, with a high-clearance four-wheel-drive vehicle required for the two passes. As a Colorado Scenic and Historic Byway and a Back Country Byway, it connects Lake City, Ouray and Silverton. CDOT highlights seven ghost towns, two high alpine passes and mountain views.

Nineteenth-century miners used these roads to haul ore in mule-drawn wagons to Silverton, Ouray and Lake City. At Animas Forks, the Gold Prince Mill briefly renewed mining investment in 1904, but closed in 1910. By 1917, most of its major parts had been taken to a new facility in Eureka; Animas Forks became a ghost town by the 1920s. Restoration in 2013–14 repaired the town’s surviving buildings.

On the Henson Creek side, County Road 20 follows the creek east from Capitol City through Henson toward Lake City. From Lake City, the loop heads west over Cinnamon Pass or Engineer Pass to Animas Forks and returns over the other side. Animas Forks lies northeast of Silverton, connected to it by an unpaved road. The full route crosses alpine tundra and mountain meadows, reaching 12,800 feet at Engineer Pass.
notice: Abandoned town sites and mining structures stand along the rocky roads.

moments.title: Capitol City
moments.text: George Lee wanted his mining town to become Colorado’s capital and himself to become governor. He founded it as Galena City in 1877, then changed the name to Capitol City to attract interest. Lee built a smelter and sawmill, while the town acquired a schoolhouse, cabins and businesses. Falling silver prices, lawsuits and difficult transportation contributed to its decline. The surviving post office, Lee’s Smelter Stack and brick kilns occupy a site surrounded by private homes and land. Its post office operated from May 18, 1877, until October 30, 1920. Lee’s own house used bricks hauled from Pueblo.
moments.notice: The post office, Lee’s Smelter Stack and brick kilns survive at the townsite.

moments.title: Henson
moments.text: A hole in the Hidden Treasure Dam marks a later chapter in Henson’s mining history. The hydroelectric dam on Henson Creek supplied power to the Ute-Ulay Mine. It burst in 1973, causing flooding and pollution downstream; the damaged structure remains visible from the road. Henson is now a ghost town and the mine is abandoned. Its post office operated from 1883 to 1913. The name itself once varied between Hansen, Hanson, Hensen and Honsen, until the Board on Geographic Names supported Henson in 1896. The settlement stands at 9,236 feet, taking its name from Henson Creek. Downstream, the creek joins the Lake Fork Gunnison River in Lake City.
moments.notice: The breached Hidden Treasure Dam is visible from the road.

moments.title: Animas Forks
moments.text: Nine standing buildings at Animas Forks have been stabilized and restored. The mining town’s first log cabin went up in 1873, and by 1876 it had 30 cabins, a hotel, a store and a saloon. In 1884, a 23-day blizzard buried it under 25 feet of snow, forcing residents to tunnel between buildings. The buildings underwent stabilization in 1997–98 and a fuller restoration in 2013–14. That work included a reconstructed gable roof for the jail, the site’s oldest building. Work on the buildings repaired floors, walls, windows and doors, restored cedar-shingle roofs on several structures and improved drainage across the site.
moments.notice: The jail’s gable roof was reconstructed during the restoration completed in 2014.

practical: Capitol City: The full Alpine Loop requires high-clearance four-wheel drive and closes in winter. CDOT advises a full tank and extra food and water. (checked 2026-10-11)
